recipe.history:
The bell pepper — Capsicum annuum — is native to Central and South America, where it has been cultivated for at least eight thousand years, making it one of the oldest domesticated crops in the Western Hemisphere. Archaeological evidence from Mexico and Peru shows that peppers were a foundational element of pre-Columbian cuisine long before any European arrived to notice them. Unlike their hotter relatives, bell peppers lost their capsaicin through a natural genetic mutation that was then selectively cultivated, resulting in a fruit of pure sweetness and mild vegetal flavor that could be eaten in quantity. The Columbian Exchange of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries carried peppers from the Americas to Europe, where they were initially regarded as ornamental curiosities before being absorbed into cooking with remarkable speed. In Hungary they became paprika; in Spain they became pimientos; in the Balkans and the Mediterranean they became roasted and preserved vegetables that remain centerpieces of those cuisines today. The three-color combination of red, yellow, and green bell peppers — each representing the same variety at different stages of ripeness — became a signature of both the Creole cooking of Louisiana and the broader American cooking vernacular of the twentieth century.

Roasted bell pepper relish found its way onto American burgers through the Italian-American sandwich tradition, where giardiniera and roasted pepper condiments were standard toppings for sausage and beef. By the late twentieth century, upscale burger restaurants were offering roasted pepper toppings as a way to add sweetness, acidity, and visual drama to their patties, and the tri-color relish — red for sweetness, yellow for fruitiness, green for grassiness and slight bitterness — became a way to achieve complexity through a single condiment. Roasting the peppers directly over an open flame or under a broiler transforms them entirely: the skin chars and slips away, revealing softened flesh that is simultaneously sweet, smoky, and acidic with the vinegar in which it is typically preserved.

The first time I roasted bell peppers over an open gas flame I was twenty-two and living in a small apartment with very little to my name but a good cast-iron skillet and a gas stove. I put a red pepper directly over the burner flame as I had seen done on television and stood there watching it blacken and blister and collapse, and when I peeled it under cold running water and tasted the silken red flesh inside I understood something new about fire and transformation. The smoky sweetness was unlike anything the raw pepper could have offered. I made a relish that night with olive oil and garlic and red wine vinegar and put it on everything for the next week — sandwiches, eggs, toast, and eventually, inevitably, burgers. It has never left my rotation. Roasted tri-color pepper relish on a burger is a gift, and it requires nothing in return except a patty cooked correctly.

A medium rare patty and a roasted pepper relish share a particular quality: they are both things that have been changed by heat in exactly the right amount. The peppers have been roasted to the point of transformation without being burned to the point of bitterness. The patty has been cooked to 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — the precise interval at which the meat has been transformed from raw to cooked without losing what makes it worth eating. Both processes are about applying the right amount of fire for exactly the right amount of time and then stopping. The burger is a meditation on restraint, and the roasted pepper relish is its most eloquent visual argument.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
For the tri-color roasted bell pepper relish:
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
1 clove garlic, minced to a paste
instructions: 1. Roast the bell peppers: Place all three peppers directly over a gas burner flame on high, or under a broiler as close to the element as possible. Turn with tongs every 2–3 minutes until the skins are completely charred and black on all sides, about 10–12 minutes total. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and let steam for 15 minutes.

2. Peel the peppers: Rub the charred skin off under cold running water or by hand — do not rinse the interior, as you want to preserve the smoky juices. Remove and discard the stems and seeds. Cut the flesh into rough strips, then roughly chop.

3. Make the relish: Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add chopped roasted peppers, red wine vinegar, sugar, smoked paprika, oregano, salt, black pepper, and red pepper flakes. Cook, stirring, for 5 minutes until the liquid reduces and the relish tightens. Remove from heat and stir in remaining olive oil and parsley. Cool to room temperature.
4. Make the aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, garlic paste, lemon juice, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper until smooth. Refrigerate until ready to use.

5. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg and mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
6. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
7. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise again until doubled, about 45 minutes.
8. Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions of about 170g each. Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
11. Lay a slice of provolone on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is fully melted.
12. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
13. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

14. Assemble: Spread smoked paprika aioli on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place romaine on the bottom bun. Set the cheesed patty on top of the lettuce. Spoon a generous mound of tri-color roasted bell pepper relish over the patty. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
